arXiv:1609.02108v1 [q-fin.MF] 07 Sep 2016

The characteristic function of rough Heston models

Omar El Euch Affiliation: CMAP, École Polytechnique Paris Email: omar.el-euch@polytechnique.edu Affiliation: Affiliation: Mathieu Rosenbaum Affiliation: CMAP, École Polytechnique Paris Email: mathieu.rosenbaum@polytechnique.edu
Abstract

It has been recently shown that rough volatility models, where the volatility is driven by a fractional Brownian motion with small Hurst parameter, provide very relevant dynamics in order to reproduce the behavior of both historical and implied volatilities. However, due to the non-Markovian nature of the fractional Brownian motion, they raise new issues when it comes to derivatives pricing. Using an original link between nearly unstable Hawkes processes and fractional volatility models, we compute the characteristic function of the log-price in rough Heston models. In the classical Heston model, the characteristic function is expressed in terms of the solution of a Riccati equation. Here we show that rough Heston models exhibit quite a similar structure, the Riccati equation being replaced by a fractional Riccati equation.

Keywords: Rough volatility models, rough Heston models, Hawkes processes, fractional Brownian motion, fractional Riccati equation, limit theorems.

1 Introduction

The celebrated Heston model is a one-dimensional stochastic volatility model where the asset price SS follows the following dynamic:

d​St=St​Vt​d​WtdS_{t}=S_{t}\sqrt{V_{t}}dW_{t}
d​Vt=λ⁡(θ−Vt)​d​t+λ​ν​Vt​d​Bt.dV_{t}=\lambda(\theta-V_{t})dt+\lambda\nu\sqrt{V_{t}}dB_{t}. (1)

Here the parameters λ\lambda, θ\theta, V0V_{0} and ν\nu are positive, and WW and BB are two Brownian motions with correlation coefficient ρ\rho, that is ⟨d​Wt,d​Bt⟩=ρ​d​t\langle dW_{t},dB_{t}\rangle=\rho dt.

The popularity of this model is probably due to three main reasons:

  • •

    It reproduces well several important stylized facts of low frequency price data, namely leverage effect, time-varying volatility and fat tails, see [7, 9, 13, 35].

  • •

    It generates very reasonable shapes and dynamics for the implied volatility surface. Indeed, the “volatility of volatility” parameter ν\nu enables us to control the smile, the correlation parameter ρ\rho to deal with the skew, and the initial volatility V0V_{0} to fix the at-the-money volatility level, see [15, 17, 30, 38]. Furthermore, as observed in markets and in contrast to local volatility models, in Heston model, the volatility smile moves in the same direction as the underlying and the forward smile does not flatten with time, see [17, 26, 27, 37].

  • •

    There is an explicit formula for the characteristic function of the asset log-price, see [23]. From this formula, efficient numerical methods have been developed, allowing for instantaneous model calibration and pricing of derivatives, see [1, 8, 31, 32].

In the classical Heston model, the volatility follows a Brownian semi-martingale. However, it is shown in [18] that for a very wide range of assets, historical volatility time-series exhibit a behavior which is much rougher than that of a Brownian motion. More precisely, dynamics of log-volatility are very well modeled by a fractional Brownian motion with Hurst parameter of order 0.10.1. Furthermore, using a fractional Brownian motion with small Hurst index also enables us to reproduce very accurately the features of the volatility surface, see [5, 18]. Finally, convincing microstructural foundations for rough volatility models are provided in [14, 28], see also Section 2.

Hence, in this paper, we are interested in the fractional versions of Heston model. Our main goal is to design an efficient pricing methodology for such models, in the spirit of the one introduced by Heston in the classical case. This is particularly important in fractional volatility models where the use of Monte-Carlo methods can be quite intricate due to the non-Markovian nature of the fractional Brownian motion, see [6].

We now define our so-called rough Heston model. Let us recall that a fractional Brownian motion WHW^{H} with Hurst parameter H∈(0,1)H\in(0,1) can be built through the Mandelbrot-van Ness representation:

WtH=1Γ⁡(H+1/2)​∫−∞0((t−s)H−12−(−s)H−12)​d​Ws+1Γ⁡(H+1/2)​∫0t(t−s)H−12​d​Ws.W_{t}^{H}=\frac{1}{\Gamma(H+1/2)}\int_{-\infty}^{0}\big((t-s)^{H-\frac{1}{2}}-(-s)^{H-\frac{1}{2}}\big)dW_{s}+\frac{1}{\Gamma(H+1/2)}\int_{0}^{t}(t-s)^{H-\frac{1}{2}}dW_{s}. (2)

The kernel (t−s)H−12(t-s)^{H-\frac{1}{2}} in (2) plays a central role in the rough dynamic of the fractional Brownian motion for H<1/2H<1/2. In particular, one can show that the process

∫0t(t−s)H−12​d​Ws\int_{0}^{t}(t-s)^{H-\frac{1}{2}}dW_{s}

has Hölder regularity H−εH-\varepsilon for any ε>0\varepsilon>0. In order to allow for a rough behavior of the volatility in a Heston-type model, we naturally introduce the kernel (t−s)α−1(t-s)^{\alpha-1} in a Heston-like stochastic volatility process as follows:

d​St=St​Vt​d​WtdS_{t}=S_{t}\sqrt{V_{t}}dW_{t}
Vt=V0+1Γ⁡(α)​∫0t(t−s)α−1​λ​(θ−Vs)​𝑑s+1Γ⁡(α)​∫0t(t−s)α−1​λ​ν​Vs​d​Bs.V_{t}=V_{0}+\frac{1}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\int_{0}^{t}(t-s)^{\alpha-1}\lambda(\theta-V_{s})ds+\frac{1}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\int_{0}^{t}(t-s)^{\alpha-1}\lambda\nu\sqrt{V_{s}}dB_{s}. (3)

The parameters λ\lambda, θ\theta, V0V_{0} and ν\nu in (3) are positive and play the same role as in (1), and here also WW and BB are two Brownian motions with correlation ρ\rho. The additional parameter α\alpha belongs to (1/2,1)(1/2,1) and governs the smoothness of the volatility sample paths. More precisely, we show in this paper that the model is well-defined and that the volatility trajectories have almost surely Hölder regularity α−1/2−ε\alpha-1/2-\varepsilon, for any ε>0\varepsilon>0. When α=1\alpha=1, Models (3) and (1) coincide, and we retrieve the classical Heston model. Therefore it is natural to view (3) as a rough version of Heston model and to call it rough Heston model. Nevertheless, note that other definitions of rough Heston models can make sense, see [19] for an alternative definition and some asymptotic results.

Our aim in this work is to derive a Heston-type formula for the characteristic function of the log-price in Model (3). In the classical case (α=1\alpha=1, Model (1)), this formula is proved in [23]. It is obtained using the fact that Model (1) is Markovian and time-homogeneous, and applying Itô’s formula to the function

L⁡(t,a,Vt,St)=𝔼⁡[ei​a​log⁡(ST)|ℱt],ℱt=σ⁡(Ws,Bs,s≤t),a∈ℝ.L(t,a,V_{t},S_{t})=\mathbb{E}[e^{ia\log(S_{T})}|{\cal{F}}_{t}],\penalty\ \penalty\ {\cal{F}}_{t}=\sigma(W_{s},B_{s};s\leq t),\penalty\ \penalty\ a\in\mathbb{R}.

The process LL being a martingale, the following Feynman-Kac partial differential equation for LL is easily obtained:

−∂tL(t,a,S,V)=(λ(θ−V)∂v+12(λν)2V∂v​v2+12S2V∂s​s2+ρνλSV∂s​v2)L(t,a,S,V),-\partial_{t}L(t,a,S,V)=\big(\lambda(\theta-V)\partial_{v}+\frac{1}{2}(\lambda\nu)^{2}V\partial_{vv}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}S^{2}V\partial_{ss}^{2}+\rho\nu\lambda SV\partial_{sv}^{2}\big)L(t,a,S,V),

with boundary condition L⁡(T,a,S,V)=ei​a​log⁡(S)L(T,a,S,V)=e^{ia\log(S)}. From this PDE, it can be checked that the characteristic function of the log-price Xt=log⁡(St/S0)X_{t}=\log(S_{t}/S_{0}) satisfies

𝔼⁡[ei​a​Xt]=exp⁡(g⁡(a,t)+V0​h​(a,t)),\mathbb{E}[e^{iaX_{t}}]=\exp\big(g(a,t)+V_{0}h(a,t)\big),

where hh is solution of the following Riccati equation:

∂th=12​(−a2−i​a)+λ⁡(i​a​ρ​ν−1)​h​(a,s)+(λ​ν)22​h2​(a,s),h⁡(a,0)=0,\partial_{t}h=\frac{1}{2}(-a^{2}-ia)+\lambda(ia\rho\nu-1)h(a,s)+\frac{(\lambda\nu)^{2}}{2}h^{2}(a,s),\penalty\ \penalty\ h(a,0)=0, (4)

and

g⁡(a,t)=θ​λ​∫0th⁡(a,s)​𝑑s.g(a,t)=\theta\lambda\int_{0}^{t}h(a,s)ds.

Solving this Riccati equation leads to the closed-form formula for the characteristic function of the log-price given in [23].

In the case α<1\alpha<1, the rough Heston model (3) is neither Markovian nor a semi-martingale. Hence the strategy initially used by Heston presented above seems very hard to adapt to our setting. Here we resort to a completely different and original approach based on point processes. Indeed, our methodology finds its root in the works [14, 28] which provide microstructural foundations to rough volatility models. In these papers, it is shown that some well-designed microstructure models, reproducing the stylized facts of modern financial markets at high frequency, give rise in the long run to rough volatility models. These microstructure models that we describe in more details in Section 2 are based on so-called nearly unstable Hawkes processes. In this paper, inspired by these results and using again Hawkes processes, we design a suitable sequence of point processes which converges to Model (3). Exploiting the specific structure of our point processes, we derive their characteristic function, which leads us in the limit to that of the log-price in the rough Heston model (3).

Our main result is that, quite surprisingly, the characteristic function of the log-price in rough Heston models exhibits the same structure as the one obtained in the classical Heston model. The difference is that the Riccati equation (4) is replaced by a fractional Riccati equation, where a fractional derivative appears instead of a classical derivative. More precisely, we obtain

𝔼⁡[ei​a​Xt]=exp⁡(g1​(a,t)+V0​g2​(a,t)),\mathbb{E}[e^{iaX_{t}}]=\exp\big(g_{1}(a,t)+V_{0}g_{2}(a,t)\big),

where

g1​(a,t)=θ​λ​∫0th⁡(a,s)​𝑑s,g2​(a,t)=I1−α​h​(a,t),g_{1}(a,t)=\theta\lambda\int_{0}^{t}h(a,s)ds,\quad g_{2}(a,t)=I^{1-\alpha}h(a,t),

and hh is a solution of the following fractional Riccati equation:

Dα​h=12​(−a2−i​a)+λ⁡(i​a​ρ​ν−1)​h​(a,s)+(λ​ν)22​h2​(a,s),I1−α​h​(a,0)=0,D^{\alpha}h=\frac{1}{2}(-a^{2}-ia)+\lambda(ia\rho\nu-1)h(a,s)+\frac{(\lambda\nu)^{2}}{2}h^{2}(a,s),\penalty\ \penalty\ I^{1-\alpha}h(a,0)=0,

with DαD^{\alpha} and I1−αI^{1-\alpha} the fractional derivative and integral operators defined in (21) and (22). Remark that when α=1\alpha=1, this result indeed coincides with the classical Heston’s result. However, note that for α<1\alpha<1, the solutions of such Riccati equations are no longer explicit. Nevertheless, they are easily solved numerically, see Section 5.

The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we build a sequence of Hawkes-type processes which converges to the rough Heston model (3). Then we study in Section 3 the characteristic function of these processes and show in Section 4 that it enables us to derive the characteristic function of the log-price in Model (3). One numerical illustration is given in Section 5 and some proofs are relegated to Section 6. Finally, some useful technical results are given in an appendix.

2 From Hawkes processes to rough Heston models

We build in this section a sequence of Hawkes-type processes which converges to the rough Heston model (3). This construction is inspired by the paper [14]. In this work, microstructural foundations for rough Heston models are provided. This is done designing suitable sequences of ultra high frequency price models which reproduce the stylized facts of modern markets microstructure and converge in the long run to rough Heston models. These microscopic price models are based on Hawkes processes. So that the reader can well understand the genesis of our original methodology to compute the characteristic function in rough Heston models, we recall here the main ideas and results in [14].

2.1 Microstructural foundations for rough Heston models

In [14], we consider a sequence of bi-dimensional Hawkes processes (NT,+,NT,−)(N^{T,+},N^{T,-}) indexed by T>0T>0 going to infinity11 1 Of course by TT we implicitly mean TnT_{n} with n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} tending to infinity. and with intensity

λtT=(λtT,+λtT,−)=μT​(11)+∫0taT​ϕ​(t−s).(d​NsT,+d​NsT,−),\lambda_{t}^{T}=\begin{pmatrix}\lambda_{t}^{T,+}\\ \lambda_{t}^{T,-}\end{pmatrix}=\mu_{T}\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 1\end{pmatrix}+\int_{0}^{t}a_{T}\phi(t-s).\begin{pmatrix}dN_{s}^{T,+}\\ dN_{s}^{T,-}\end{pmatrix}, (5)

with

ϕ=(φ1φ3φ2φ4).\phi=\begin{pmatrix}\varphi_{1}&\varphi_{3}\\ \varphi_{2}&\varphi_{4}\end{pmatrix}.

Here the φi\varphi_{i} are measurable non-negative deterministic functions and μT\mu_{T} and 0<aT<10<a_{T}<1 are some deterministic sequences of positive real numbers, see [3] and the references therein for more details about the definition of Hawkes processes. Then in [14], inspired by [2, 3, 29], we consider the following ultra high frequency tick-by-tick model for the transaction price PtTP_{t}^{T}:

PtT=NtT,+−NtT,−.P_{t}^{T}=N_{t}^{T,+}-N_{t}^{T,-}.

Hence NtT,+N_{t}^{T,+} represents the number of upward jumps of one tick of the transaction price over the period [0,t][0,t] and NtT,−N_{t}^{T,-} the number of downward jumps. The relevance of this Hawkes-based modeling is that it enables us to encode very easily the most important stylized facts of high frequency markets in term of the parameters of the Hawkes process. We now give these stylized facts and their translation in term of the model parameters, referring to [14] for more details.

  • •

    Markets are highly endogenous: In the high frequency trading context, most orders have no real economic motivation. They are rather sent by algorithms as reaction to other orders. In the Hawkes framework, this amounts to work with so-called nearly unstable Hawkes processes. This means that the stability condition

    𝒮⁡(∫0∞aT​ϕ​(s)​𝑑s)<1,\mathcal{S}\big(\int_{0}^{\infty}a_{T}\phi(s)ds\big)<1,

    where 𝒮\mathcal{S} denotes the spectral radius operator, should almost be saturated and that the intensity of exogenous orders, namely μT\mu_{T}, should be small, see [14, 20, 28, 29]. In term of model parameters, suitable constraints are therefore

    aT→1,𝒮⁡(∫0∞ϕ⁡(s)​𝑑s)=1,μT→0.a_{T}\rightarrow 1,\penalty\ \penalty\ \mathcal{S}\big(\int_{0}^{\infty}\phi(s)ds\big)=1,\penalty\ \penalty\ \mu_{T}\rightarrow 0.
  • •

    It is not an easy task to make money with high frequency strategies on highly liquid electronic markets. Hence some “no statistical arbitrage” mechanisms should be in force. We translate this assuming that in the long run, there are on average as many upward than downward jumps. This corresponds to the assumption

    φ1+φ3=φ2+φ4.\varphi_{1}+\varphi_{3}=\varphi_{2}+\varphi_{4}.
  • •

    Buying is not the same action as selling. This means that buy market orders and sell limit orders are not symmetric orders. To see this, consider for example a market maker, with an inventory which is typically positive. He is likely to raise the price by less following a buy order than to lower the price following the same size sell order. Indeed, its inventory becomes smaller after a buy order, which is a good thing for him, whereas it increases after a sell order. This creates a liquidity asymmetry on the bid and ask sides of the order book. This can be modeled in the Hawkes framework assuming that

    φ3=β​φ2,\varphi_{3}=\beta\varphi_{2},

    for some β>1\beta>1. Hence, the matrix ϕ\phi finally takes the form

    ϕ=(φ1β​φ2φ2φ1+(β−1)​φ2).\phi=\begin{pmatrix}\varphi_{1}&\beta\varphi_{2}\\ \varphi_{2}&\varphi_{1}+(\beta-1)\varphi_{2}\end{pmatrix}.
  • •

    A significant amount of transactions is part of metaorders, which are large orders whose execution is split in time by trading algorithms. This is translated into a heavy tail assumption on the functions φ1\varphi_{1} and φ2\varphi_{2}, namely that there exists 1/2<α<11/2<\alpha<1 (typically around 0.6 in practice, see [4, 20]) and C>0C>0 such that

    α​xα​∫x∞φ1​(s)+β​φ2​(s)​𝑑s​→x→∞​C.\alpha x^{\alpha}\int_{x}^{\infty}\varphi_{1}(s)+\beta\varphi_{2}(s)ds\underset{x\rightarrow\infty}{\rightarrow}C.

    Furthermore, it is shown in [28] that for a given α\alpha, there is only one way to make μT\mu_{T} tends to zero and aTa_{T} tends to one so that the limit of the price is not degenerate. More precisely,

    (1−aT)​Tα​→T→∞​λ∗,μT​T1−α​→T→∞​μ,(1-a_{T})T^{\alpha}\underset{T\rightarrow\infty}{\rightarrow}\lambda^{*},\penalty\ \penalty\ \mu_{T}T^{1-\alpha}\underset{T\rightarrow\infty}{\rightarrow}\mu,

    for some positive λ∗\lambda^{*} and μ\mu.

Under the above assumptions, it is proved in [14] that the properly rescaled microscopic price process

1−aTμ​Tα​Pt​TT,t∈[0,1]\sqrt{\frac{1-a_{T}}{\mu T^{\alpha}}}P_{tT}^{T},\penalty\ \penalty\ t\in[0,1]

converges in law as TT tends to infinity to the following macroscopic price dynamic PtP_{t}:

Pt=21−∫0∞(φ1−φ2)​∫0tσs​d​Ws,P_{t}=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{1-\int_{0}^{\infty}(\varphi_{1}-\varphi_{2})}\int_{0}^{t}\sigma_{s}dW_{s},
σt2=1Γ⁡(α)​∫0t(t−s)α−1​λ​(1−σs2)​𝑑s+1Γ⁡(α)​λ​ν​∫0t(t−s)α−1​σs​d​Bs,\sigma_{t}^{2}=\frac{1}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\int_{0}^{t}(t-s)^{\alpha-1}\lambda(1-\sigma_{s}^{2})ds+\frac{1}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\lambda\nu\int_{0}^{t}(t-s)^{\alpha-1}\sigma_{s}dB_{s}, (6)

where (W,B)(W,B) is a bi-dimensional correlated Brownian motion with correlation

ρ=1−β2​(1+β2)\rho=\frac{1-\beta}{\sqrt{2(1+\beta^{2})}}

and

ν=2​(1+β2)λ∗​μ​(1+β)2,λ=λ∗​αC​Γ​(1−α).\nu=\sqrt{\frac{2(1+\beta^{2})}{\lambda^{*}\mu(1+\beta)^{2}}},\penalty\ \penalty\ \lambda=\lambda^{*}\frac{\alpha}{C\Gamma(1-\alpha)}.

Hence this result shows that the main stylized facts of modern electronic markets naturally give rise to a very rough behavior of the volatility. Indeed, recall that the Hurst parameter corresponds to α−1/2\alpha-1/2.

Inspired by this result, our idea is to study the characteristic function of some kind of microscopic price processes in order to deduce that of our rough Heston macroscopic price of interest (3). However, the developments presented above cannot be directly applied and need to be adapted. Indeed, remark that in (6), σ0=0\sigma_{0}=0. This does not correspond to the case of (3), where having a non-zero initial volatility is of course crucial for the model to be relevant in practice. Thus we need to modify the sequence of Hawkes-type processes to obtain a non-degenerate initial volatility in the limit. This is actually a non-trivial issue. However, this can be achieved replacing μT\mu_{T} in (5) by an inhomogeneous Poisson intensity μ^T​(t)\hat{\mu}_{T}(t). We explain how such μ^T​(t)\hat{\mu}_{T}(t) can be found in the next section.

2.2 Finding the right Poisson rate

We work on a sequence of probability spaces (ΩT,ℱT,ℙT)({\Omega}^{T},{\cal{F}}^{T},{\mathbb{P}}^{T}), indexed by T>1T>1, on which NT=(NT,+,NT,−)N^{T}=(N^{T,+},N^{T,-}) is a bi-dimensional Hawkes process with intensity:

λtT=(λtT,+λtT,−)=μ^T​(t)​(11)+∫0tϕT​(t−s).d​NsT.\lambda_{t}^{T}=\begin{pmatrix}\lambda_{t}^{T,+}\\ \lambda_{t}^{T,-}\end{pmatrix}=\hat{\mu}_{T}(t)\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 1\end{pmatrix}+\int_{0}^{t}\phi^{T}(t-s).dN_{s}^{T}. (7)

For a given TT, the probability space is equipped with the filtration (ℱtT)t≥0(\mathcal{F}_{t}^{T})_{t\geq 0}, where ℱtT\mathcal{F}_{t}^{T} is the σ\sigma-algebra generated by (NsT)s≤t(N_{s}^{T})_{s\leq t}. Since our goal is to design a sequence of processes leading in the limit to a rough Heston dynamic, we consider the same kind of assumptions on the matrix ϕT\phi^{T} as those described in the previous section. However, here we can be very specific since we just need to find one convenient sequence of processes. That is why we make a particular choice for the heavy-tailed functions defining ϕT\phi^{T}, using Mittag-Leffler functions, see Section A.1 in Appendix for definition and some properties. Indeed, these functions are very convenient in order to carry out computations. More precisely, our assumptions on ϕT\phi^{T} are as follows.

Assumption 2.1.

There exist β≥0\beta\geq 0, 1/2<α<11/2<\alpha<1 and λ>0\lambda>0 such that

aT=1−λ​T−α,ϕT=φT​χ,a_{T}=1-\lambda T^{-\alpha},\penalty\ \penalty\ \phi^{T}=\varphi^{T}\chi,

where

χ=1β+1​(1β1β),φT=aT​φ,φ=fα,1,\chi=\frac{1}{\beta+1}\begin{pmatrix}1&\beta\\ 1&\beta\end{pmatrix},\penalty\ \penalty\ \varphi^{T}=a_{T}\varphi,\penalty\ \penalty\ \varphi=f^{\alpha,1},

with fα,1f^{\alpha,1} the Mittag-Leffler density function defined in Appendix.

Remark 2.1.

As in the previous section, we are working in the nearly unstable heavy tail case since

∫0∞φ⁡(s)​𝑑s=1\int_{0}^{\infty}\varphi(s)ds=1

and

α​xα​∫x∞φ⁡(t)​𝑑t​⟶x→∞​αΓ⁡(1−α).\alpha x^{\alpha}\int_{x}^{\infty}\varphi(t)dt\underset{x\rightarrow\infty}{\longrightarrow}\frac{\alpha}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)}.

We now give intuitions on how to find a suitable Poisson intensity μ^T​(t)\hat{\mu}_{T}(t). The developments here are not very rigorous. They just aim at helping the reader to understand how our point processes sequence is designed. First, note that under Assumption 2.1,

λtT,+=λtT,−.\lambda_{t}^{T,+}=\lambda_{t}^{T,-}.

The asymptotic behavior of the renormalized intensity processes λtT,+\lambda_{t}^{T,+} and λtT,−\lambda_{t}^{T,-} will give us that of the volatility in our limiting macroscopic price model. Thus, we need to understand the long term limit of λtT,+\lambda_{t}^{T,+}. Let us write

MtT=(MtT,+,MtT,−)=NtT−∫0tλsT​𝑑sM_{t}^{T}=(M_{t}^{T,+},M_{t}^{T,-})=N_{t}^{T}-\int_{0}^{t}\lambda_{s}^{T}ds

for the martingale associated to the point process NtTN_{t}^{T}. We easily obtain

λtT,+=μ^T​(t)+∫0tφT​(t−s)​λsT,+​𝑑s+11+β​∫0tφT​(t−s)​(d​MsT,++β​d​MsT,−).\lambda_{t}^{T,+}=\hat{\mu}_{T}(t)+\int_{0}^{t}\varphi^{T}(t-s)\lambda_{s}^{T,+}ds+\frac{1}{1+\beta}\int_{0}^{t}\varphi^{T}(t-s)(dM_{s}^{T,+}+\beta dM_{s}^{T,-}).

Now let

ψT=∑k≥1(φT)∗k,\psi^{T}=\sum_{k\geq 1}(\varphi^{T})^{*k},

where (φT)∗1=φT(\varphi^{T})^{*1}=\varphi^{T} and for k>1k>1, (φT)∗k​(t)=∫0tφT​(s)​(φT)∗(k−1)​(t−s)​𝑑s(\varphi^{T})^{*k}(t)=\int_{0}^{t}\varphi^{T}(s)(\varphi^{T})^{*(k-1)}(t-s)ds. Using Lemma A.1 in Appendix together with Fubini theorem and the fact that ψT∗φT=ψT−φT\psi^{T}*\varphi^{T}=\psi^{T}-\varphi^{T}, we get

λtT,+=μ^T​(t)+∫0tψT​(t−s)​μ^T​(s)​𝑑s+11+β​∫0tψT​(t−s)​(d​MsT,++β​d​MsT,−).\lambda_{t}^{T,+}=\hat{\mu}_{T}(t)+\int_{0}^{t}\psi^{T}(t-s)\hat{\mu}_{T}(s)ds+\frac{1}{1+\beta}\int_{0}^{t}\psi^{T}(t-s)(dM_{s}^{T,+}+\beta dM_{s}^{T,-}). (8)

In light of the preceding computations, we consider from now on the following assumption.

Assumption 2.2.

The baseline intensity μ^T\hat{\mu}_{T} is given by

μ^T​(t)=μT+ξ​μT​(11−aT​(1−∫0tφT​(s)​𝑑s)−∫0tφT​(s)​𝑑s),\hat{\mu}_{T}(t)=\mu_{T}+\xi\mu_{T}\big(\frac{1}{1-a_{T}}(1-\int_{0}^{t}\varphi^{T}(s)ds)-\int_{0}^{t}\varphi^{T}(s)ds\big),

with ξ>0\xi>0 and μT=μ​Tα−1\mu_{T}=\mu T^{\alpha-1} for some μ>0\mu>0.

Remark 2.2.

Note that μ^T\hat{\mu}_{T} can also be written as follows:

μ^T​(t)=μT+ξ​μT​(Tαλ​∫t∞φ⁡(s)​𝑑s+λ​T−α​∫0tφ⁡(s)​𝑑s).\hat{\mu}_{T}(t)=\mu_{T}+\xi\mu_{T}\big(\frac{T^{\alpha}}{\lambda}\int_{t}^{\infty}\varphi(s)ds+\lambda T^{-\alpha}\int_{0}^{t}\varphi(s)ds\big).

This shows that μ^T\hat{\mu}_{T} is a positive function and thus that the intensity process λtT\lambda_{t}^{T} in (7) is well-defined.

2.3 The rough limits of Hawkes processes

We now give a rigorous statement about the limiting behavior of our specific sequence of bi-dimensional nearly unstable Hawkes processes with heavy tails. For t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1], we define

XtT=1−aTTα​μ​Nt​TT,ΛtT=1−aTTα​μ​∫0t​TλsT​𝑑s,ZtT=Tα​μ1−aT​(XtT−ΛtT).X_{t}^{T}=\frac{1-a_{T}}{T^{\alpha}\mu}N_{tT}^{T},\penalty\ \penalty\ \Lambda_{t}^{T}=\frac{1-a_{T}}{T^{\alpha}\mu}\int_{0}^{tT}\lambda_{s}^{T}ds,\penalty\ \penalty\ Z_{t}^{T}=\sqrt{\frac{T^{\alpha}\mu}{1-a_{T}}}(X_{t}^{T}-\Lambda_{t}^{T}).

Using a similar approach as that in [14], we obtain the following result whose proof is given in Section 6.

Theorem 2.1.

As T→∞T\rightarrow\infty, under Assumptions 2.1 and 2.2, the process (ΛtT,XtT,ZtT)t∈[0,1]\big(\Lambda_{t}^{T},X_{t}^{T},Z_{t}^{T}\big)_{t\in[0,1]} converges in law for the Skorokhod topology to (Λ,X,Z)(\Lambda,X,Z) where

Λt=Xt=∫0tYs​𝑑s​(11),Zt=∫0tYs​(d​Bs1d​Bs2),\Lambda_{t}=X_{t}=\int_{0}^{t}Y_{s}ds\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 1\end{pmatrix},\penalty\ \penalty\ Z_{t}=\int_{0}^{t}\sqrt{Y_{s}}\begin{pmatrix}dB_{s}^{1}\\ dB_{s}^{2}\end{pmatrix},

and YY is the unique solution of the rough stochastic differential equation

Yt=ξ+1Γ⁡(α)​∫0t(t−s)α−1​λ​(1−Ys)​𝑑s+λ​1+β2λ​μ​(1+β2)​1Γ⁡(α)​∫0t(t−s)α−1​Ys​d​Bs,Y_{t}=\xi+\frac{1}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\int_{0}^{t}(t-s)^{\alpha-1}\lambda(1-Y_{s})ds+\lambda\sqrt{\frac{1+\beta^{2}}{\lambda\mu(1+\beta^{2})}}\frac{1}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\int_{0}^{t}(t-s)^{\alpha-1}\sqrt{Y_{s}}dB_{s},

where

B=B1+β​B21+β2B=\frac{B^{1}+\beta B^{2}}{\sqrt{1+\beta^{2}}}

and (B1,B2)(B^{1},B^{2}) is a bi-dimensional Brownian motion. Furthermore, for any ε>0\varepsilon>0, YY has Hölder regularity α−1/2−ε\alpha-1/2-\varepsilon.

Hence Theorem 2.1 shows that designing our sequence of bi-dimensional Hawkes processes in a suitable way, its limit is differentiable and its derivative exhibits a rough Cox-Ingersoll-Ross like behavior, with non-zero initial value. This is exactly what we need for the limiting volatility of our microscopic price processes. Indeed, thanks to Theorem 2.1, we are now able to build such microscopic processes converging to the log-price in (3). More precisely, for θ>0\theta>0, let us define

PT=θ21−aTTα​μ(N.TT,+−N.TT,−)−θ21−aTTα​μN.TT,+=θ2(ZT,+−ZT,−)−θ2XT,+.P^{T}=\sqrt{\frac{\theta}{2}}\sqrt{\frac{1-a_{T}}{T^{\alpha}\mu}}(N_{.T}^{T,+}-N_{.T}^{T,-})-\frac{\theta}{2}\frac{1-a_{T}}{T^{\alpha}\mu}N_{.T}^{T,+}=\sqrt{\frac{\theta}{2}}(Z^{T,+}-Z^{T,-})-\frac{\theta}{2}X^{T,+}. (14)

We have the following corollary of Theorem 2.1.

Corollary 2.1.

As T→∞T\rightarrow\infty, under Assumptions 2.1 and 2.2, the sequence of processes (PtT)t∈[0,1](P_{t}^{T})_{t\in[0,1]} converges in law for the Skorokhod topology to

Pt=∫0tVs​d​Ws−12​∫0tVs​𝑑s,P_{t}=\int_{0}^{t}\sqrt{V_{s}}dW_{s}-\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{t}V_{s}ds,

where VV is the unique solution of the rough stochastic differential equation

Vt=θ​ξ+1Γ⁡(α)​∫0t(t−s)α−1​λ​(θ−Vs)​𝑑s+λ​θ⁡(1+β2)λ​μ​(1+β)2​1Γ⁡(α)​∫0t(t−s)α−1​Vs​d​Bs,V_{t}=\theta\xi+\frac{1}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\int_{0}^{t}(t-s)^{\alpha-1}\lambda(\theta-V_{s})ds+\lambda\sqrt{\frac{\theta(1+\beta^{2})}{\lambda\mu(1+\beta)^{2}}}\frac{1}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\int_{0}^{t}(t-s)^{\alpha-1}\sqrt{V_{s}}dB_{s},

with (W,B)(W,B) a correlated bi-dimensional Brownian motion whose bracket satisfies

d​⟨W,B⟩t=1−β2​(1+β2)​d​t.d\langle W,B\rangle_{t}=\frac{1-\beta}{\sqrt{2(1+\beta^{2})}}dt.

Thus, we have succeeded in building a sequence of microscopic processes PTP^{T}, defined by (14), which converges to (the logarithm of) our rough Heston process of interest (3). Now our goal is to use the result of Corollary 2.1 to compute the characteristic function of the log-price in the rough Heston model (3). This is done in the next two sections.

3 The characteristic function of multivariate Hawkes processes

We have seen in the previous section that our sequence of Hawkes-based microscopic price processes converges to the log-price in the rough Heston model (3). Therefore, if we are able to compute the characteristic function for the microscopic price, its limit will give us that of the log-price in a rough Heston model. We actually provide a more general result here, deriving the characteristic function of a multivariate Hawkes process (recall that a bi-dimensional Hawkes process is the building block for our microscopic price process (14)). Hence we extend here some results already proved in [22] in the one-dimensional case.

3.1 Cluster-based representation

To derive our characteristic function, the representation of Hawkes processes in term of clusters, see [22], is very useful. We recall it now. Let us consider a dd-dimensional Hawkes process N=(N1,…,Nd)N=(N^{1},...,N^{d}) with intensity

λt=(λt1λtd)=μ⁡(t)+∫0tϕ⁡(t−s).d​Ns,\lambda_{t}=\begin{pmatrix}\lambda_{t}^{1}\\ \vdots\\ \lambda_{t}^{d}\end{pmatrix}=\mu(t)+\int_{0}^{t}\phi(t-s).dN_{s}, (15)

where μ:ℝ+→ℝ+d\mu:\mathbb{R}_{+}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{+}^{d} is locally integrable and ϕ:ℝ+→ℳd​(ℛ+)\phi:\mathbb{R}_{+}\rightarrow\cal{M}^{\textbf{d}}(\mathbb{R}_{+}) has integrable components such that

𝒮⁡(∫0∞ϕ⁡(s)​𝑑s)<1.\mathcal{S}\big(\int_{0}^{\infty}\phi(s)ds\big)<1.

The law of such process can be described through a population approach. Consider that there are dd types of individuals and for a given type, an individual can be either a migrant or the descendant of a migrant. Then the dynamic goes as follows from time t=0t=0:

  • •

    Migrants of type k∈{1,..,d}k\in\{1,..,d\} arrive as a non-homogenous Poisson process with rate μk​(t)\mu_{k}(t).

  • •

    Each migrant of type k∈{1,..,d}k\in\{1,..,d\} gives birth to children of type j∈{1,..,d}j\in\{1,..,d\} following a non-homogenous Poisson process with rate ϕj,k​(t)\phi_{j,k}(t).

  • •

    Each child of type k∈{1,..,d}k\in\{1,..,d\} also gives birth to other children of type j∈{1,..,d}j\in\{1,..,d\} following a non-homogenous Poisson process with rate ϕj,k​(t)\phi_{j,k}(t).

Then, for k∈{1,..,d}k\in\{1,..,d\}, NtkN_{t}^{k} can be taken as the number up to time tt of migrants and children born with type kk. Indeed, the population approach above and the theoretical characterization (15) define the same point process law.

3.2 The result

Let L⁡(a,t)L(a,t) be the characteristic function of the Hawkes process NN:

L(a,t)=𝔼[exp(ia.Nt)],t≥0,a∈ℝd,L(a,t)=\mathbb{E}[\exp(ia.N_{t})],\penalty\ \penalty\ t\geq 0,\penalty\ \penalty\ a\in\mathbb{R}^{d},

where a.Nta.N_{t} stands for the scalar product of aa and NtN_{t}. The cluster-based representation of multivariate Hawkes processes enables us to show the following result, proved in Section 3.3, for their characteristic function.

Theorem 3.1.

We have

L(a,t)=exp(∫0t(C(a,t−s)−𝟏).μ(s)ds),L(a,t)=\exp\big(\int_{0}^{t}\big(C(a,t-s)-\mathbf{1}\big).\mu(s)ds\big),

where C:ℝd×ℝ+→ℂdC:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}_{+}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{d} is solution of the following integral equation:

C(a,t)=exp(ia+∫0tϕ∗(s).(C(a,t−s)−𝟏)ds),C(a,t)=\exp\big(ia+\int_{0}^{t}\phi^{*}(s).(C(a,t-s)-\mathbf{1})ds\big),

with ϕ∗​(s)\phi^{*}(s) the transpose of ϕ⁡(s)\phi(s).

From Theorem 3.1, we are able to derive in Section 4 the characteristic function of rough Heston models.

3.3 Proof of Theorem 3.1

We now give the proof of Theorem 3.1, exploiting the population construction presented in Section 3.1. We start by defining dd auxiliary independent dd-dimensional point processes (N~k,j)1≤j≤d(\tilde{N}^{k,j})_{1\leq j\leq d}, k∈{1,…,d}k\in\{1,...,d\}, defined as follows for each given k∈{1,..,d}k\in\{1,..,d\}:

  • •

    Migrants of type j∈{1,…,d}j\in\{1,...,d\} arrive as a non-homogenous Poisson process with rate ϕj,k​(t)\phi_{j,k}(t).

  • •

    Each migrant of type j∈{1,..,d}j\in\{1,..,d\} gives birth to children of type l∈{1,..,d}l\in\{1,..,d\} following a non-homogenous Poisson process with rate ϕl,j​(t)\phi_{l,j}(t).

  • •

    Each child of type j∈{1,..,d}j\in\{1,..,d\} also gives birth to other children of type l∈{1,..,d}l\in\{1,..,d\} following a non-homogenous Poisson process with rate ϕl,j​(t)\phi_{l,j}(t).

For a given k∈{1,..,d}k\in\{1,..,d\}, N~tk,j\tilde{N}_{t}^{k,j} corresponds to the number, up to time tt, of migrants and children with type jj. A simple but crucial remark is that (N~k,j)1≤j≤d(\tilde{N}^{k,j})_{1\leq j\leq d} is actually also a multivariate Hawkes process with migrant rate (ϕj,k)1≤j≤d(\phi_{j,k})_{1\leq j\leq d} and kernel matrix ϕ\phi. We write Lk​(a,t)L_{k}(a,t) for its characteristic function

Lk(a,t)=𝔼[exp(ia.(N~tk,j)1≤j≤d)],t≥0,a∈ℝd.L_{k}(a,t)=\mathbb{E}\big[\exp(ia.(\tilde{N}_{t}^{k,j})_{1\leq j\leq d})\big],\penalty\ \penalty\ t\geq 0,\penalty\ \penalty\ a\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

Now let us come back to the initial Hawkes process of interest NN defined by (15). For each k∈{1,…,d}k\in\{1,...,d\} and t≥0t\geq 0, let Nt0,kN_{t}^{0,k} be the number of its migrants of type kk arrived up to time tt. Recall that the N0,kN^{0,k}, 1≤k≤d1\leq k\leq d, are independent Poisson processes with rates μk​(t)\mu_{k}(t). We also define T1k<…<TNt0,kk∈[0,t]T_{1}^{k}<...<T_{N_{t}^{0,k}}^{k}\in[0,t] the arrival times of migrants of type kk of the Hawkes process NN, up to time tt. Using the population approach presented in Section 3.1, it is clear that at time tt, the number of descendants of different types of a migrant of type kk arrived at time TukT_{u}^{k} has the same law as (N~t−Tukk,j)1≤j≤d(\tilde{N}_{t-T_{u}^{k}}^{k,j})_{1\leq j\leq d}, where N~\tilde{N} is taken independent from NN. Consequently,

4 The characteristic function of rough Heston models

We give in this section our main theorem, that is the characteristic function for the log-price in rough Heston models (3). It is obtained combining the convergence result for Hawkes processes stated in Corollary 2.1 together with the characteristic function for multivariate Hawkes processes derived in Theorem 3.1. We start with some intuitions about the result.

with g=μ⁡(c+d)g=\mu(c+d). We give in the next section a rigorous statement for this result.

4.2 Main result

We define the fractional integral of order r∈(0,1]r\in(0,1] of a function ff as

Ir​f​(t)=1Γ⁡(r)​∫0t(t−s)r−1​f​(s)​𝑑s,I^{r}f(t)=\frac{1}{\Gamma(r)}\int_{0}^{t}(t-s)^{r-1}f(s)ds, (21)

whenever the integral exists, and the fractional derivative of order r∈[0,1)r\in[0,1) as

Dr​f​(t)=1Γ⁡(1−r)​dd​t​∫0t(t−s)−r​f​(s)​𝑑s,D^{r}f(t)=\frac{1}{\Gamma(1-r)}\frac{d}{dt}\int_{0}^{t}(t-s)^{-r}f(s)ds, (22)

whenever it exists. The following theorem, proved in Section 6, is the main result of the paper.

Theorem 4.1.

Consider the rough Heston model (3) with a correlation between the two Brownian motions ρ\rho satisfying ρ∈(−1/2,1/2]\rho\in(-1/\sqrt{2},1/\sqrt{2}]. For all t≥0t\geq 0, we have

Lp​(a,t)=exp⁡(θ​λ​I1​h​(a,t)+V0​I1−α​h​(a,t)),L_{p}(a,t)=\exp\big(\theta\lambda I^{1}h(a,t)+V_{0}I^{1-\alpha}h(a,t)\big), (23)

where hh is solution of the fractional Riccati equation

Dα​h​(a,t)=12​(−a2−i​a)+λ⁡(i​a​ρ​ν−1)​h​(a,s)+(λ​ν)22​h2​(a,s),I1−α​h​(a,0)=0,D^{\alpha}h(a,t)=\frac{1}{2}(-a^{2}-ia)+\lambda(ia\rho\nu-1)h(a,s)+\frac{(\lambda\nu)^{2}}{2}h^{2}(a,s),\penalty\ \penalty\ I^{1-\alpha}h(a,0)=0, (24)

which admits a unique continuous solution.

Thus we have been able to obtain a semi-closed formula for the characteristic function in rough Heston models. This means that pricing of European options becomes an easy task in this model, see Section 5. For α=1\alpha=1, we retrieve the classical Heston formula. For α<1\alpha<1, the formula is almost the same. The difference is essentially only in that in the Riccati equation, the classical derivative is replaced by a fractional derivative. The drawback is that such fractional Riccati equations do not have explicit solutions. However, they can be solved numerically almost instantaneously, see Section 5. Finally, note that this strong link between Hawkes processes and (rough) Heston models is probably natural since both of them exhibit some kind of affine structure (although infinite-dimensional).

5 Numerical application

5.1 Numerical scheme

We explain in this section how to compute numerically the characteristic function of the log-price in a rough Heston model. By Theorem 4.1, Lp​(a,t)L_{p}(a,t) is entirely defined through the fractional Riccati equation (24)

Dα​h​(a,t)=F⁡(a,h⁡(a,t)),I1−α​h​(a,0)=0,D^{\alpha}h(a,t)=F\big(a,h(a,t)\big),\penalty\ \penalty\ I^{1-\alpha}h(a,0)=0,

where

F⁡(a,x)=12​(−a2−i​a)+λ⁡(i​a​ρ​ν−1)​x+(λ​ν)22​x2.F(a,x)=\frac{1}{2}(-a^{2}-ia)+\lambda(ia\rho\nu-1)x+\frac{(\lambda\nu)^{2}}{2}x^{2}.

Several schemes for solving numerically (24) can be found in the literature. Most of them are based on the idea that (24) implies the following Volterra equation:

h⁡(a,t)=1Γ⁡(α)​∫0t(t−s)α−1​F​(a,h⁡(a,s))​𝑑s.h(a,t)=\frac{1}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\int_{0}^{t}(t-s)^{\alpha-1}F\big(a,h(a,s)\big)ds. (25)

Then one develops numerical schemes for (25). Here we choose the well-known fractional Adams method investigated in [10, 11, 12]. The idea goes as follows. Let us write g⁡(a,t)=F⁡(a,h⁡(a,t))g(a,t)=F\big(a,h(a,t)\big). Over a regular discrete time-grid (tk)k∈ℕ(t_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} with mesh Δ\Delta (tk=k​Δ)(t_{k}=k\Delta), we estimate

h⁡(a,tk+1)=1Γ⁡(α)​∫0tk+1(tk+1−s)α−1​g​(a,s)​𝑑sh(a,t_{k+1})=\frac{1}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\int_{0}^{t_{k+1}}(t_{k+1}-s)^{\alpha-1}g(a,s)ds

by

1Γ⁡(α)​∫0tk+1(tk+1−s)α−1​g^​(a,s)​𝑑s,\frac{1}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\int_{0}^{t_{k+1}}(t_{k+1}-s)^{\alpha-1}\hat{g}(a,s)ds,

where

g^​(a,t)=tj+1−ttj+1−tj​g^​(a,tj)+t−tjtj+1−tj​g^​(a,tj+1),t∈[tj,tj+1), 0≤j≤k.\hat{g}(a,t)=\frac{t_{j+1}-t}{t_{j+1}-t_{j}}\hat{g}(a,t_{j})+\frac{t-t_{j}}{t_{j+1}-t_{j}}\hat{g}(a,t_{j+1}),\penalty\ \penalty\ t\in[t_{j},t_{j+1}),\penalty\ \penalty\ 0\leq j\leq k.

This corresponds to a trapezoidal discretization of the fractional integral and leads to the following scheme:

h^​(a,tk+1)=∑0≤j≤kaj,k+1​F​(a,h^​(a,tj))+ak+1,k+1​F​(a,h^​(a,tk+1)),\hat{h}(a,t_{k+1})=\sum_{0\leq j\leq k}a_{j,k+1}F\big(a,\hat{h}(a,t_{j})\big)+a_{k+1,k+1}F\big(a,\hat{h}(a,t_{k+1})\big), (26)

with

a0,k+1=ΔαΓ⁡(α+2)​(kα+1−(k−α)​(k+1)α),a_{0,k+1}=\frac{\Delta^{\alpha}}{\Gamma(\alpha+2)}\big(k^{\alpha+1}-(k-\alpha)(k+1)^{\alpha}\big),
aj,k+1=ΔαΓ⁡(α+2)​((k−j+2)α+1+(k−j)α+1−2​(k−j+1)α+1), 1≤j≤k,a_{j,k+1}=\frac{\Delta^{\alpha}}{\Gamma(\alpha+2)}\big((k-j+2)^{\alpha+1}+(k-j)^{\alpha+1}-2(k-j+1)^{\alpha+1}\big),\penalty\ \penalty\ 1\leq j\leq k, (27)

and

ak+1,k+1=ΔαΓ⁡(α+2).a_{k+1,k+1}=\frac{\Delta^{\alpha}}{\Gamma(\alpha+2)}.

However, h^​(a,tk+1)\hat{h}(a,t_{k+1}) being on both sides of (26), this scheme is implicit. Thus, in a first step, we compute a pre-estimation of h^​(a,tk+1)\hat{h}(a,t_{k+1}) based on a Riemann sum that we then plug into the trapezoidal quadrature. This pre-estimation, called predictor and that we denote by h^P​(a,tk+1)\hat{h}^{P}(a,t_{k+1}) is defined by

h^P​(a,tk+1)=1Γ⁡(α)​∫0t(t−s)α−1​g~​(a,s)​𝑑s,\hat{h}^{P}(a,t_{k+1})=\frac{1}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\int_{0}^{t}(t-s)^{\alpha-1}\tilde{g}(a,s)ds,

with

5.2 One numerical illustration

We consider the rough Heston model (3) with the following parameters:

λ=2,ρ=−0.5,V0=0.4,ν=0.05,θ=0.04.\lambda=2,\penalty\ \penalty\ \rho=-0.5,\penalty\ \penalty\ V_{0}=0.4,\penalty\ \penalty\ \nu=0.05,\penalty\ \penalty\ \theta=0.04.

To compute Lp​(a,t)L_{p}(a,t), we use the numerical scheme presented above to solve Riccati equation and then plug the numerical solution into (23). Once the characteristic function is obtained, classical methods are available to obtain call prices

C⁡(K,T)=𝔼​[ST−K]+,C(K,T)=\mathbb{E}[S_{T}-K]_{+},

see [8, 24, 32] and the survey [41]. In our case, we use Lewis method, see [32]. Here we display the term structure of the at-the-money skew, that is the derivative of the implied volatility with respect to log-strike for at-the-money calls. We compute it for α=1\alpha=1 (classical Heston) and α=0.6\alpha=0.6 (rough Heston with Hurst parameter equal to 0.1).

We see that in the rough case, the skew explodes when maturity goes to zero, whereas it remains flat in the classical Heston case. This is a remarkable feature of rough-volatility models, very important for practical applications, see [5, 16, 28].

In the sequel, cc denotes a constant that may vary from line to line.

6.1 Proof of Theorem 2.1

The proof of Theorem 2.1 is close to the one given in [14] for the convergence of a microscopic price model to a Heston-like dynamic. The main difference is that we have to deal here with a time-varying baseline intensity μ^T\hat{\mu}_{T}, which we have introduced to get a non-zero initial volatility in the limit. As in [14], we start by showing the C-tightness of (ΛT,XT,ZT)(\Lambda^{T},X^{T},Z^{T}).

∎

6.2.3 End of the proof of Theorem 4.1

Let a∈ℝa\in\mathbb{R}. Recall that from Section 4.1, we have

and furthermore, from Proposition 6.5,

In addition, using Proposition 6.4, we get that for given t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1] and for any s∈[0,t]s\in[0,t]

|Tα​(YT,+​(a,t−s)−1)+Tα​(YT,−​(a,t−s)−1)|​(T1−α​μ^​(s​T))≤c⁡(a)​(1+s−α).\big|T^{\alpha}(Y^{T,+}(a,t-s)-1)+T^{\alpha}(Y^{T,-}(a,t-s)-1)\big|\big(T^{1-\alpha}\hat{\mu}(sT)\big)\leq c(a)(1+s^{-\alpha}).

The right hand side of the last inequality is integrable over [0,t][0,t]. Therefore, using the convergence of LT​(aT+,aT−,t​T)L^{T}(a_{T}^{+},a_{T}^{-},tT) towards Lp​(a,t)L_{p}(a,t) and applying the dominated convergence theorem, we obtain

where g⁡(a,t)=μ⁡(c⁡(a,t)+d⁡(a,t))g(a,t)=\mu\big(c(a,t)+d(a,t)\big). Thus, we have shown that

Lp​(a,t)=exp⁡(∫0tg⁡(a,s)​𝑑s+V0θ​λ​I1−α​g​(a,t)).L_{p}(a,t)=\exp\big(\int_{0}^{t}g(a,s)ds+\frac{V_{0}}{\theta\lambda}I^{1-\alpha}g(a,t)\big).

with

For a given a∈ℝa\in\mathbb{R}, consider two continuous solutions h1(a,.)h_{1}(a,.) and h2(a,.)h_{2}(a,.) of (24) or equivalently of (31). We have that |h1​(a,t)−h2​(a,t)||h_{1}(a,t)-h_{2}(a,t)| is smaller than

Appendix A Appendix

We gather in this section some useful technical results.

A.1 Mittag-Leffler functions

Let (α,β)∈(ℝ+∗)2(\alpha,\beta)\in(\mathbb{R}_{+}^{*})^{2}. The Mittag-Leffler function Eα,βE_{\alpha,\beta} is defined for z∈ℂz\in\mathbb{C} by

Eα,β​(z)=∑n≥0znΓ⁡(α​n+β).E_{\alpha,\beta}(z)=\sum_{n\geq 0}\frac{z^{n}}{\Gamma(\alpha n+\beta)}.

For (α,λ)∈(0,1)×ℝ+(\alpha,\lambda)\in(0,1)\times\mathbb{R}_{+}, we also define

fα,λ​(t)=λ​tα−1​Eα,α​(−λ​tα),t>0,f^{\alpha,\lambda}(t)=\lambda t^{\alpha-1}E_{\alpha,\alpha}(-\lambda t^{\alpha}),\penalty\ \penalty\ t>0,
Fα,λ=∫0tfα,λ​(s)​𝑑s,t≥0.F^{\alpha,\lambda}=\int_{0}^{t}f^{\alpha,\lambda}(s)ds,\penalty\ \penalty\ t\geq 0.

The function fα,λf^{\alpha,\lambda} is a density function on ℝ+\mathbb{R}_{+} called Mittag-Leffler density function. The following properties of fα,λf^{\alpha,\lambda} and Fα,λF^{\alpha,\lambda} can be found in [21, 34, 36]. We have

fα,λ​(t)​∼t→0+​λΓ⁡(α)​tα−1,fα,λ​(t)​∼t→∞​αλ​Γ​(1−α)​t−(α+1)f^{\alpha,\lambda}(t)\underset{t\rightarrow 0^{+}}{\sim}\frac{\lambda}{\Gamma(\alpha)}t^{\alpha-1},\penalty\ \penalty\ f^{\alpha,\lambda}(t)\underset{t\rightarrow\infty}{\sim}\frac{\alpha}{\lambda\Gamma(1-\alpha)}t^{-(\alpha+1)}

and

Fα,λ​(t)=1−Eα,1​(−λ​tα),Fα,λ​(t)​∼t→0+​λΓ⁡(α+1)​tα, 1−Fα,λ​(t)​∼t→∞​1λ​Γ​(1−α)​t−α.F^{\alpha,\lambda}(t)=1-E_{\alpha,1}(-\lambda t^{\alpha}),\penalty\ \penalty\ F^{\alpha,\lambda}(t)\underset{t\rightarrow 0^{+}}{\sim}\frac{\lambda}{\Gamma(\alpha+1)}t^{\alpha},\penalty\ \penalty\ 1-F^{\alpha,\lambda}(t)\underset{t\rightarrow\infty}{\sim}\frac{1}{\lambda\Gamma(1-\alpha)}t^{-\alpha}.

Finally, for α∈(1/2,1)\alpha\in(1/2,1), fα,λf^{\alpha,\lambda} is square-integrable and its Laplace transform is given for z≥0z\geq 0 by

f^α,λ​(z)=∫0∞fα,λ​(s)​e−z​s​𝑑s=λλ+zα.\hat{f}^{\alpha,\lambda}(z)=\int_{0}^{\infty}f_{\alpha,\lambda}(s)e^{-zs}ds=\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+z^{\alpha}}.

A.2 Wiener-Hopf equations

The following result is used extensively in this work to solve Wiener-Hopf type equations, see for example [3].

Lemma A.1.

Let gg be a measurable locally bounded function from ℝ\mathbb{R} to ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} and ϕ:ℝ+→ℳd​(ℛ)\phi:\mathbb{R}_{+}\rightarrow\cal{M}^{\textbf{d}}(\mathbb{R}) be a matrix-valued function with integrable components such that 𝒮⁡(∫0∞ϕ⁡(s)​𝑑s)<1\mathcal{S}(\int_{0}^{\infty}\phi(s)ds)<1. Then there exists a unique locally bounded function ff from ℝ\mathbb{R} to ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} solution of

f⁡(t)=g⁡(t)+∫0tϕ⁡(t−s).f⁡(s)​𝑑s,t≥0f(t)=g(t)+\int_{0}^{t}\phi(t-s).f(s)ds,\penalty\ \penalty\ t\geq 0

given by

f⁡(t)=g⁡(t)+∫0tψ⁡(t−s).g⁡(s)​𝑑s,t≥0,f(t)=g(t)+\int_{0}^{t}\psi(t-s).g(s)ds,\penalty\ \penalty\ t\geq 0,

where ψ=∑k≥1ϕ∗k\displaystyle\psi=\sum_{k\geq 1}\phi^{*k}.

A.3 Fractional differential equations

We end this appendix with some useful results about fractional differential equations. The next lemma can be found in [40].

Lemma A.2.

Let hh be a continuous function from [0,1][0,1] to ℝ\mathbb{R}, α∈(0,1]\alpha\in(0,1] and λ∈ℝ\lambda\in\mathbb{R}. There is a unique continuous solution to the equation

Dα​y​(t)=λ​y​(t)+h⁡(t),I1−α​y​(0)=0D^{\alpha}y(t)=\lambda y(t)+h(t),\penalty\ \penalty\ I^{1-\alpha}y(0)=0

given by

y⁡(t)=∫0t(t−s)α−1​Eα,α​(λ​(t−s)α)​h​(s)​𝑑s.y(t)=\int_{0}^{t}(t-s)^{\alpha-1}E_{\alpha,\alpha}\big(\lambda(t-s)^{\alpha}\big)h(s)ds.

We also have the following useful result.

Lemma A.3.

Let hh be a non-negative continuous function from [0,1][0,1] to ℝ\mathbb{R} such that for any t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1],

h⁡(t)≤ε+C​∫0tfα,λ​(t−s)​h​(s)​𝑑s,h(t)\leq\varepsilon+C\int_{0}^{t}f^{\alpha,\lambda}(t-s)h(s)ds,

for some ε≥0\varepsilon\geq 0 and C≥0C\geq 0. Then for any t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1],

h⁡(t)≤C′​ε,h(t)\leq C^{\prime}\varepsilon,

with

C′=1+C​λ​∫01sα−1​Eα,α​(λ⁡(C−1)​sα)​𝑑s>0.C^{\prime}=1+C\lambda\int_{0}^{1}s^{\alpha-1}E_{\alpha,\alpha}\big(\lambda(C-1)s^{\alpha}\big)ds>0.

In particular, if ε=0\varepsilon=0 then h=0h=0.

Proof:

Let

f⁡(t)=h⁡(t)−C​∫0tfα,λ​(t−s)​h​(s)​𝑑s.f(t)=h(t)-C\int_{0}^{t}f^{\alpha,\lambda}(t-s)h(s)ds.

and g=h−fg=h-f. The function gg is solution of

g⁡(t)=C​∫0tfα,λ​(t−s)​(g⁡(s)+f⁡(s))​𝑑s.g(t)=C\int_{0}^{t}f^{\alpha,\lambda}(t-s)\big(g(s)+f(s)\big)ds.

Thus, from Lemma A.2, gg is the unique solution of

Dα​g​(t)=λ⁡(C−1)​g​(t)+C​λ​f​(t),I1−α​g​(0)=0.D^{\alpha}g(t)=\lambda(C-1)g(t)+C\lambda f(t),\penalty\ \penalty\ I^{1-\alpha}g(0)=0.

Hence using again Lemma A.2, we deduce that

g⁡(t)=C​λ​∫0t(t−s)α−1​Eα,α​(λ⁡(C−1)​(t−s)α)​f​(s)​𝑑s.g(t)=C\lambda\int_{0}^{t}(t-s)^{\alpha-1}E_{\alpha,\alpha}\big(\lambda(C-1)(t-s)^{\alpha}\big)f(s)ds.

Therefore,

g⁡(t)≤C​λ​ε​∫0tsα−1​Eα,α​(λ⁡(C−1)​sα)​𝑑s.g(t)\leq C\lambda\varepsilon\int_{0}^{t}s^{\alpha-1}E_{\alpha,\alpha}\big(\lambda(C-1)s^{\alpha}\big)ds.

Using that h=f+gh=f+g together with the fact that Eα,αE_{\alpha,\alpha} is non-negative, we get the result. ∎
